0c1160d31848.headline: Moon Spuds Pass the Taste-Safety Test: Potatoes Grown in Fake Lunar Soil Are Safe to Eat
body: Potatoes grown in simulated moon soil are safe to eat, according to a new study from Oregon State University in the US, reported by Metro. The research, published in the journal npj Microgravity, suggests the humble spud could be a serious contender for future lunar menus.

The team, led by Professor Aymeric Goyer of the university's College of Agricultural Sciences and backed by Nasa funding, planted potatoes in lunar regolith simulants. Regolith is the loose rock and dust covering most of the moon's surface, and it contains very little organic matter. The researchers mixed in different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich amendment made by using earthworms to break down organic material.

The amount mattered. Plants grown in simulants with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those raised in Earth soil. Plants with no amendment were described as severely impaired, with stunting and underdeveloped roots, while those with 5% to 15% vermicompost recovered only partially.

Because moon dirt differs from place to place, the team tested five simulants representing both lunar mare and highland regions. They also grew potatoes in soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for the highest potato yields in the world, as an Earth benchmark.

Safety was the other big question. Lunar regolith contains elevated levels of heavy metals, but the researchers believe organic matter helps by binding them, reducing damage to roots and growth. They found no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, the natural potato toxins often linked to green discolouration under the skin.

The findings fit Nasa's Artemis goal of a sustained human presence on the moon, which would be far easier if food were produced there rather than shipped from Earth at great cost. The researchers say astronauts could carry a small amount of organic matter and then make more by converting food scraps and plant waste. Potatoes were chosen because they yield more calories per unit of land than many crops and are considered a practical staple for long missions.
0c1160d31848.summary: Oregon State University researchers found potatoes grown in simulated moon soil enriched with vermicompost matched Earth-grown plants and showed no significant rise in toxins, a step toward growing food for long lunar missions.
0c1160d31848.pixel_take: The Martian proved potatoes can survive on another world. Now science says the moon version won't poison you. Mash, boil, stick them in a lunar stew: the space race just got carb-loaded.
0c1160d31848.why_it_matters: Resupplying a lunar base from Earth is hugely expensive, so any way to grow food on site could cut mission costs. That matters for the commercial and government space sector, and for anyone watching the economics of long-term space exploration.
key_points: Potatoes in simulated lunar soil with 30% vermicompost grew as well as in Earth soil.
No statistically significant rise in glycoalkaloid toxins was found, despite heavy metals in regolith.
The work supports Nasa's Artemis aim of producing food on the moon instead of relying on resupply.

The story ended harmlessly, as far as the report indicates, with the source of the scare identified as AI rather than an actual reptile lurking in the plumbing. Still, it is a reminder to pause before trusting a dramatic image, especially one that shows up without context.

9329f8e154dd.headline: Big Bao Swallows Little Bao in a Cosmic Pac-Man Merger Near Andromeda
body: Astronomers have caught a giant star eating its smaller companion on the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, according to a new paper in the journal Nature. The merged star has been nicknamed Bao, and it may have been effectively rejuvenated by the meal.

The victim, dubbed Little Bao, had about 0.7 times the mass of the Sun. Its host, Big Bao, was a supergiant roughly seven times the Sun's mass, with a radius 350 times larger and a brightness about 18,000 times greater. Lead author Viraj Karambelkar's team says the pair had orbited each other for thousands of years before the collision.

What makes this special is the timing. Stellar mergers are hard to predict, so they are rarely seen live. The team flagged something odd in February 2023, using data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. Later telescopes tracked the star brightening and shedding dust, and the Zwicky Transient Facility recorded the eruption on 17 October 2025.

The James Webb Space Telescope then observed Bao on 24 December 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. The researchers say that is the earliest follow-up of an event like this. Webb's mid-infrared data revealed the dust the larger star had released over hundreds of years.

The merger also moved fast. Once Little Bao touched the giant's surface, it took only seven orbits, about seven years, to finish the job. Other known mergers involving smaller stars have taken thousands of orbits. Co-author Kishalay De described it as almost like a bomb going off inside a living star.

The process is called common envelope evolution. Sometimes both stars survive and later become neutron stars, black holes, supernovae, gravitational-wave sources or millisecond pulsars. Here, simulations showed Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao's core. Scientists say more observations are needed to pin down Bao's final properties.
9329f8e154dd.summary: Astronomers watched a supergiant star swallow a smaller companion near Andromeda, with the James Webb Space Telescope capturing the aftermath just 47 days after the eruption peaked, according to a new Nature paper.
9329f8e154dd.pixel_take: Little Bao went from binary partner to main course in seven years. Somewhere, a very patient supergiant is still chewing, and astronomers are taking notes.
9329f8e154dd.why_it_matters: Rapid-response space observation is a growing field, and this event shows how coordinated telescope networks and fast data pipelines can catch fleeting events. Better models of stellar mergers also feed into understanding black holes and gravitational waves, which drive long-term science and tech investment.
key_points: A supergiant about 7 times the Sun's mass swallowed a 0.7-solar-mass companion near Andromeda.
Webb observed the merged star, Bao, just 47 days after the eruption peaked, the earliest such follow-up.
The merger took about seven years, far faster than other known mergers involving smaller stars.

aa820a7101e6.headline: Married 58 Years and Sharing One Wallet: Why Do So Many Couples Split Their Money?
body: A reader writing to MarketWatch's money advice column says he has been married for 58 years and has always treated the household finances as "our" money, not "his" and "hers." The question he raises is why so many couples today keep their finances separate.

According to the teaser, his wife stopped working outside the home in 1970. That detail frames his view: in his marriage, one partner's paycheck was the family's paycheck, and the idea of dividing it into separate accounts never came up. The full text of the column was not available to us, so we can't report what answer, if any, the columnist gave.

The question still points to a real debate in personal finance. Some couples pool everything into joint accounts, others keep separate accounts, and many land on a hybrid, with a shared account for bills and individual accounts for personal spending. Each setup has its fans, and each can work when both partners are open about it.

Money is also one of the most common sources of tension in relationships, and secrecy tends to make it worse. Whether accounts are joint or separate, the habit that matters most is knowing where the household stands: what is owed, what is saved and what the plan is for retirement.

The letter also shows how much has changed in six decades. Arrangements where one spouse works outside the home and the other manages the household were common in 1970. Today, two-income households are far more common, and many partners arrive with their own savings, debts and financial habits, which makes separate accounts feel natural to some.
aa820a7101e6.summary: A reader married for 58 years asks MarketWatch why so many couples keep separate finances when he has always treated money as shared. The question opens a broader debate on how couples manage money.
aa820a7101e6.pixel_take: Fifty-eight years, one shared pot, zero 'who ate my share of the savings' disputes. Some couples split the bill; this one apparently split nothing and called it a day.
aa820a7101e6.why_it_matters: How couples structure their money affects savings, debt management and retirement planning. Joint and separate setups each carry trade-offs, and communication about money often matters more than the account structure itself.
key_points: A reader married 58 years says all money is shared, not 'his' and 'hers.'
His wife stopped working outside the home in 1970, per the teaser.
He asks why so many couples keep finances separate today.

dd69b1a0f5d6.headline: Pepper Pileup: Truck Sheds 19 Pallets of Peppers, Closing Two Lanes of Busy Florida Road
body: A truck lost 19 pallets of peppers onto a busy road in Florida, forcing authorities to temporarily close two lanes, according to UPI. The spill turned an ordinary stretch of pavement into an unplanned produce aisle.

The material available gives few details beyond that: the number of pallets, the type of cargo and the lane closures. It does not say which road was affected, how long the lanes stayed shut, what caused the load to fall, or whether anyone was hurt, so we will not guess.

What is clear is that a load of 19 pallets is no small thing. Pallets of produce are heavy and bulky, and they can't be nudged aside by hand like a dropped grocery bag. Clearing them typically takes crews, equipment and time, which is why lanes get closed while cleanup happens.

Spills like this are a small reminder of how much of the food supply chain rides on trucks. When a load comes off, the cost can include the lost cargo, traffic delays for commuters and cleanup work. Who bears those costs depends on the specifics, which were not reported here.
For drivers, the lesson is the usual one: when traffic suddenly slows and the road ahead looks colorful, it may not be a festival. It may just be dinner, on the asphalt.

dd69b1a0f5d6.why_it_matters: Trucks carry most fresh food, so one lost load means wasted cargo, traffic delays and cleanup costs. Small incidents like this show how fragile and road-dependent the supply chain can be, and those costs can eventually feed into prices.

bd585bf0c402.headline: Toronto Police and Firefighters Chase Escaped Chickens Around a Parking Lot
body: Police and firefighters in Toronto were called to a parking lot to round up more than a dozen chickens that had escaped from a van, according to UPI. The scene was captured in a video the outlet shared.

Details are thin. The material available does not say exactly when the birds broke out, how they got loose, who owned them, or whether every one of them was eventually caught. We are also not told where the van was headed.

What we do know is that emergency crews, who usually deal with far graver emergencies, were pulled into a very different kind of pursuit. Chasing a flock of chickens across pavement is not in most job descriptions, yet two separate services turned up for it.

Loose livestock in an urban setting is a genuine public-safety concern, even when it looks funny. Birds darting around a parking lot can startle drivers and pedestrians, and a van full of animals that has lost part of its cargo raises basic questions about how the animals were being transported.
For now, the story stands as a quirky reminder that city life occasionally throws in a curveball with feathers. No injuries or charges were mentioned in the information available.
bd585bf0c402.summary: Police and firefighters in Toronto responded to a parking lot to corral more than a dozen chickens that escaped from a van, UPI reported, sharing video of the chase.

bd585bf0c402.why_it_matters: Small oddities like this show how logistics, even for something as ordinary as moving animals by van, can go sideways and pull in public resources. Every emergency call costs taxpayer-funded time, and transport mishaps can mean losses for the businesses involved.

d009dab7d650.headline: School Bets on Prize Draw to Keep Pupils From Ditching Class for 'GTA VI'
body: A school in Northern Ireland is trying a creative tactic to keep students in their seats when "Grand Theft Auto VI" arrives: a prize drawing for pupils who show up, according to UPI.

The idea is simple. Instead of relying only on warnings and lectures, the school is dangling the chance to win prizes in front of pupils who might otherwise be tempted to stay home and play the game. The material available does not specify what the prizes are, how many there are, or the exact rules of the draw.

It is a classic piece of incentive design. Attendance is the goal, a hugely anticipated video game is the temptation, and a raffle is the counterweight. Whether a shot at a prize can compete with a title many fans have waited years to play is the open question.

The story also shows how big game launches have become cultural events that reach well beyond gaming. When a release is big enough that a school feels the need to plan around it, it is a sign of just how much attention the franchise commands.
No results have been reported yet, so it remains to be seen whether the drawing actually keeps pupils in class.

7959f46d944f.headline: Passenger sues driver over chicken-induced braking, loses and is ordered to pay costs
body: A woman in Singapore who sued her private-hire driver after he braked hard to avoid a car that had stopped for a chicken has lost her case. According to Metro, citing CNA, she was ordered to pay S$15,000 (about £8,700) in legal costs.

The incident happened on February 19, 2024, on Holland Road. Ms Yvonne Chen Qianyun was a passenger in a car driven by Mr Tan Teng Kiat. A chicken wandered in front of the vehicle ahead, which braked, and Mr Tan then braked too to avoid hitting it.

Ms Chen, whose injuries were not specified in the judgment, sued for negligence. She argued he had not left enough space and had stopped more forcefully than needed. Mr Tan said he was driving at around 50km/h, about 10 metres behind the other car, and had enough room and time to stop safely.

He also told the court that Ms Chen had first asked whether he had noted the number plate of the car in front, because she wanted to pursue that driver over her worsening back pain. He said she even asked him to be a witness, before later deciding to sue him instead.

Judge Ng noted that Ms Chen had at least two other cases pending in the district court, both over separate road accidents: one in September 2022 involving a private-hire car, and one in October 2024 involving her husband's car. She was a passenger in both.

The judge accepted she was an innocent passenger, but said the driver was not to blame. The law, the judge said, does not look for someone at fault for every loss, and some losses must lie where they fall. The chicken crossing was, in the judge's words, part of the 'vicissitudes of life'.
7959f46d944f.summary: A Singapore passenger who sued her private-hire driver for braking to avoid a chicken-related stop lost her case and must pay S$15,000 in costs. The judge called it part of life's vicissitudes.
7959f46d944f.pixel_take: The chicken crossed the road, the court crossed out the claim, and the passenger got a very expensive answer to the age-old question of why.
7959f46d944f.why_it_matters: The ruling shows that courts won't treat every accident as someone's fault, and that a failed lawsuit can cost far more than it was meant to recover. Legal costs can be a real financial risk for anyone considering a claim, and they also bear on insurance and ride-hailing liability.
key_points: Claim over a driver's sudden braking to avoid a chicken-related stop was dismissed in Singapore.
The claimant must pay S$15,000 (about £8,700) in costs.
The judge called the incident part of the 'vicissitudes of life' and found the driver not to blame.

245e983eeaa9.headline: Stray Dog Reportedly Joins Coyote Pack, Gets Caught on Arizona Yard Cameras
body: An Arizona woman who set up wildlife cameras to record the animals passing through her yard ended up documenting something she apparently didn't expect: a dog running with a pack of coyotes, according to UPI.

The report, published in mid-November 2026, describes the dog as a stray. Beyond the headline and a short teaser, the details are thin. The material available does not say how long the dog was with the coyotes, how the animals interacted, or what happened to the dog afterward.

What we can say is that the woman's cameras, installed for ordinary wildlife watching, captured an unusual case of a dog and coyotes apparently traveling together. Dogs and coyotes are close relatives, which is why the two can sometimes look alike at a glance, but a dog actually integrating with a wild pack is rare enough to make the news.

The story is a reminder of how much backyard trail cameras now reveal. Cheap, motion-triggered devices have turned ordinary homeowners into amateur field researchers, and their footage regularly shows wildlife behavior that would once have gone unseen. In this case, the camera caught a social oddity: a stray that appears to have found a new crowd.

e5d3309454e1.headline: Airline Clears Up Baggage Mystery: That Brown Goo Was Peanut Butter, Not Poop
body: American Airlines says the brown substance that left some passengers worried about their luggage was liquefied peanut butter, not human waste, according to a report from UPI.

The explanation came after passengers feared the smear coating their bags was something far less appetizing. The airline's verdict: it was a spreadable snack that had melted and gone rogue, not a biological hazard.

The material available gives few other details. It does not say how much luggage was affected, where it happened, how the peanut butter escaped its container, or what the airline offered affected travelers, so we will not guess.

Still, the episode shows how fast a mystery stain can spiral into a full-blown panic. When something brown shows up on a suitcase, imagination tends to skip the pantry and head straight for the worst-case scenario.

For travelers, the lesson is a practical one. Liquids and semi-liquids can leak in transit, and a jar of anything spreadable is a gamble in a cargo hold. Wrapping messy items in sealed bags is cheap insurance against an awkward baggage-claim moment.
e5d3309454e1.summary: American Airlines said the brown substance that alarmed some passengers on their bags was liquefied peanut butter, not human waste, according to UPI.

Some passengers had feared it was human waste.

f85bf9d03644.headline: Small Dog Gets Wedged Between Shipping Containers at California Schoolyard, Gets Rescued
body: A small dog ran between two shipping containers at a California schoolyard and got stuck, prompting a rescue by firefighters and animal rescuers, according to UPI.

The material available is brief. It confirms that firefighters and animal rescue workers responded to the schoolyard and that the dog became wedged in the gap. The headline says the dog was rescued. Shipping containers are built to be stacked, trucked and shipped, not to leave comfortable room for a curious pet. Even a narrow gap between two steel boxes can turn into a tight spot, because a small animal can squeeze in and then be unable to turn around or back out.

Stories like this tend to end well when trained crews are called quickly, and the headline suggests this one did. Rescue teams often handle animal calls like this, and the case is a reminder that a pet's curiosity can create a real emergency within seconds.
UPI described the scene as a schoolyard, but the teaser gives no further detail about the location, the dog's owner or whether anyone else was involved.

39e3d33fb9cf.headline: Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, the farthest any human-made object has ever strayed
body: NASA's Voyager 1 probe has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, according to UPI. That makes it the first human-made object in space to get that far from home.

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us, so a signal from Voyager 1 now needs a full day to cross the gap. Send it a message and you will wait roughly a day for it to arrive, then another day for the reply.

The milestone caps a decades-long journey. UPI reports that the probe has explored both the solar system and the interstellar medium beyond it, the thin space between stars that lies outside the Sun's immediate influence.

The material available for this story is brief, so details on the exact date of the crossing and the probe's current condition are not covered here. The headline fact is simple: nothing built by humans has ever been this far away.

For context, Voyager 1 is a veteran of an era when spacecraft were built to last on very modest computing power. It is a reminder that long-term engineering, patience and a good dose of luck can outlast several generations of gadgets, most of which struggle to survive a phone upgrade cycle.
39e3d33fb9cf.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth, a distance light needs 24 hours to cross, according to UPI.
39e3d33fb9cf.pixel_take: Voyager 1 is so far away that even its replies to 'u up?' arrive a day late. Still more reliable than most of our gadgets after two years.
39e3d33fb9cf.why_it_matters: Voyager 1 shows the payoff of long-horizon investment in space science and engineering durability. Data from interstellar space can't be gathered any other way, and it informs future deep-space mission design, a field with growing commercial and government interest.
key_points: Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth, a first for any human-made object.
Signals take about 24 hours to travel one way at that distance.
The probe has explored both the solar system and interstellar space, per UPI.

d5056aa77c07.headline: London's Newest Estate Agent Sells Gingerbread Homes, and the Only Mortgage Is Your Sweet Tooth
body: A gingerbread 'estate agent' has opened in Bloomsbury, central London, offering visitors a look at miniature edible houses. According to Metro, the pop-up, called Crumbs, Coffee & Co, opens on November 18 at 43 Store Street.

The tiny properties were made by baker Jenny Pasha, who spent 150 hours crafting houses that reflect popular architectural styles found across London. The star attraction is a model of the Shard, which on its own took 60 hours of baking and building.

The project is a promotional stunt from Nescafé. The brand says a survey found Brits name gingerbread as their favourite winter flavour, ahead of cinnamon, salted caramel, pumpkin spice and spiced apple.

The timing is deliberate: Nescafé is bringing back its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after a ten-year break, which it says followed fan petitions and social media requests. Visitors can collect a freshly brewed one for free, and entry to the pop-up costs nothing.

Ingrid Hayes, marketing director for Nescafé UK and Ireland, said research shows people want simple, affordable ways to bring joy to their winter routine. She said the pop-up gives fans an immersive way to celebrate the flavour while bringing café-style warmth into their own kitchens.
d5056aa77c07.summary: Nescafé has opened a free gingerbread 'estate agent' pop-up in Bloomsbury, London, showing handmade edible houses and a Shard model, to launch the return of its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after ten years.
d5056aa77c07.pixel_take: Finally, a London property with no bidding wars, no chain collapses and no survey needed. The only damp is the icing, and the only deposit is a latte you get free.
d5056aa77c07.why_it_matters: Brands are leaning on immersive pop-ups and nostalgia to make seasonal products feel like events, often cheaper than traditional advertising and perfect for social sharing. For shoppers, it shows how consumer sentiment about 'affordable joy' is shaping marketing in the coffee aisle.
key_points: Crumbs, Coffee & Co opens November 18 at 43 Store Street, Bloomsbury, with free entry.
Baker Jenny Pasha spent 150 hours on the houses, including 60 hours on a Shard replica.
Nescafé is reviving its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after ten years and giving away free cups.

d8f91bd27568.headline: Sheep on the Lam: Fugitive Flock-Member Eludes Connecticut Police and Animal Wranglers for Days
body: A sheep that bolted shortly after arriving at its new owner's home in Connecticut remains at large, according to UPI. Police and animal wranglers say the animal has not been seen in days, despite efforts to track it down.

The details are thin: the material available does not say where in Connecticut the escape happened, how the sheep got away, or exactly when. What is reported is the basic plot. New home, new owner, and apparently a very quick decision that the arrangement was not for the sheep.

Police and animal wranglers have been involved in the search, which suggests the owner is not the only one hoping for a happy ending. So far, the sheep has proven better at hiding than anyone has proven at finding it.

Stories like this are a reminder that moving day is stressful for every species. Animals taken to unfamiliar surroundings can panic and run, and a frightened animal in open country can be difficult to locate and even harder to approach.

For now there is no word on a capture, and no update on the sheep's condition. If anyone in the area spots a wandering woolly runaway, the sensible move is presumably to contact the authorities already working the case rather than freelance a rodeo.
d8f91bd27568.summary: A sheep escaped shortly after arriving at its new owner's Connecticut home and has not been seen in days, police and animal wranglers told UPI. The search continues.

key_points: A sheep escaped shortly after arriving at its new owner's home in Connecticut.
Police and animal wranglers say it has not been seen in days.
No capture has been reported, per UPI.

676b4edb8443.headline: Estonian trail camera spots a 'unicorn' deer, and no, it isn't a horse with a dental plan
body: A trail camera on an island in Estonia has recorded video of a roe deer that appears to have a single antler growing from the middle of its forehead, according to UPI. The animal has been nicknamed a "unicorn" online.

The footage shows the deer with what resembles one central horn-like growth, rather than the usual pair of antlers mounted on either side of the head. The material available does not say exactly when the video was captured, who operates the camera, or what caused the unusual look.

Because the details are thin, it is worth being careful about what we can say. The report describes the growth only as something resembling a single antler. Why it looks that way has not been explained in the information we have, so any diagnosis would be guesswork.

What we can say is that trail cameras have become a quiet engine of wildlife discovery. Cheap, motion-triggered and battery-powered, they let researchers, hunters and hobbyists capture animals that would never behave naturally with a human standing nearby. Every so often they catch something that goes viral, and a one-antlered deer is a perfect candidate.

For now, the Estonian unicorn remains a charming oddity: a reminder that nature does not always follow the template, and that a motion sensor in the woods can occasionally out-deliver a fantasy novel.
676b4edb8443.summary: A trail camera on an Estonian island filmed a roe deer with what looks like a single antler on its forehead, earning it the nickname 'unicorn', UPI reports.
676b4edb8443.pixel_take: Finally, a unicorn that's low-maintenance: no glitter, no rainbow, just one antler and a motion sensor that caught it doing deer things.

The animal has been nicknamed a 'unicorn', according to UPI.
The cause of the unusual growth was not given in the available material.

7797d9dd4147.headline: Idaho Man Juggles His Way Through 19 Miles on In-Line Skates for World Record
body: An Idaho man who already holds multiple Guinness World Records for juggling has taken on what he describes as his toughest challenge yet: juggling while rolling along on in-line skates for 19 miles, according to UPI.

Doing both at once, for a distance that rivals a long-distance run, is a very different sort of workout.

UPI's short report, which includes video, does not provide further details in the material available to us, such as the man's name, the exact time it took, or whether Guinness has formally certified the result. We will update the story if more details emerge.

Guinness World Records has long been a home for this kind of niche athleticism, where the goal is not to be the best at a famous sport but the only person on Earth crazy enough to try a specific combination.

af980158c300.headline: Dorchester Honors Susie the Wandering Cat With a Bronze Statue Fit for a Local Celebrity
body: A town in England has done what many cat owners already believe is overdue: it has cast a feline in bronze. Locals in Dorchester gathered for the unveiling of a statue of Susie, a wandering cat described as one of the town's most beloved residents, according to UPI.

With millions of players buying tickets, someone is bound to land a repeat prize eventually, and those stories make headlines precisely because they are rare to any one person.

For the rest of us, the lesson is the usual one. Lottery games are designed so that the house, in this case state lottery proceeds, comes out ahead over time. Scratch-offs are fun, but a financial plan built on them is more of a hobby than a strategy.

A loose animal in a narrow aisle can complicate boarding, seating and safety checks, and crews typically want things settled before the aircraft leaves the gate.

c84df890b210.headline: Kalshi's 'perps' now out-trade its prediction markets, and the casino-turned-exchange has a new favorite game
body: Kalshi, best known for letting people bet on sports, politics and culture, has hit a milestone: its perpetual futures, or "perps," topped the notional trading volume of its event contracts on two consecutive days, according to CNBC. The product launched in May.

On Thursday, perps saw $3.4 billion in notional volume, versus about $3 billion for prediction markets. That was the day Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the broader market sold off. Perps also edged ahead on one day in September, and then again on Friday.

Perps are futures-style contracts with no expiration date. Traders don't need to own the underlying asset, and funding payments between long and short holders keep the contract price in line with the market. Notably, perps volume includes any leverage traders take on, while event contracts are fully collateralized, for now, CNBC noted.

Kalshi was first to list perps in the U.S., after winning federal approval in May for crypto-linked contracts. It has since been cleared for metals, crude oil, stock indexes and individual stocks, and on Monday it launched contracts tied to Anthropic. Udesh Jha of Kalshi Klear, its clearing house, pointed to offshore perps, which generated more than $90 trillion in notional volume in 2025, as a reason for the rapid growth.

Not everyone is cheering. CME Group is suing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission over the approval, and some incumbent exchanges saw their shares fall after perps were cleared. CNBC previously reported that volume on Kalshi's bitcoin and ether perps far exceeded open interest, which is unusual for regulated futures. Kalshi said it has "zero concerns" about that.

Kalshi's near-monopoly on U.S. perps may not last. Coinbase has filed to list single-stock perps, and President Donald Trump said in August that the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid to domestic traders. Analyst Owen Lau of Clear Street sees single-stock perps as the biggest growth opportunity. CNBC disclosed it has a commercial relationship with Kalshi, including a minority investment.
c84df890b210.summary: Kalshi's perpetual futures topped the trading volume of its prediction markets for a second straight day, CNBC reports. Expansion into single-stock perps, and rising competition and legal challenges, will shape what comes next.
c84df890b210.pixel_take: Kalshi built its name on betting on what happens next, and now its side hustle is outselling the main act. Even prediction markets didn't see that one coming.
c84df890b210.why_it_matters: Perps bring leveraged, always-on trading of stocks, commodities and crypto into the U.S. regulated arena, challenging traditional futures exchanges. Leverage amplifies both gains and losses, so retail traders should understand the risks. The CME lawsuit and incoming rivals could reshape who profits.
key_points: Kalshi perps hit $3.4 billion in notional volume Thursday, topping about $3 billion for prediction markets.
Kalshi now has approval for perps on crypto, metals, oil, stock indexes and individual stocks.
CME is suing the CFTC over the approval, and Coinbase and Hyperliquid are positioning to compete.

fbae9cff9d2d.headline: Al Gore, Hometown Hero, Adds 'Newspaper Owner' to a Résumé Already Heavy on Vice Presidents
body: The Carthage Courier, a weekly newspaper in Carthage, Tennessee, announced this week that former Vice President Al Gore is buying the paper, according to The New York Times. The Courier has been publishing since 1913.

The headline the Times chose describes the buyer as "Carthage Resident Al Gore," which suggests the local framing matters here: this is a hometown paper getting a hometown owner. The material available does not include the purchase price, the terms of the deal, or any plans Gore has for the paper, so those details remain unknown.

Still, the move fits a larger story in American media. Local newspapers have spent years under pressure as print advertising shrank and readers moved online, and many weeklies have been sold, merged or closed. A paper that has made it past a century of publishing is something of a survivor.

Small-town weeklies tend to cover the things bigger outlets skip, such as county meetings, school boards, high school sports and local business. When they vanish, that coverage often goes with them, which is why a new owner with a personal stake in the community can be a notable development for readers.

Whether Gore will take an active role in running the Courier, or what the purchase signals about his business interests, has not been spelled out in the information we have. We will update this story if more details emerge.
fbae9cff9d2d.summary: Former Vice President Al Gore is buying the Carthage Courier, a Tennessee weekly published since 1913, the paper announced this week, according to The New York Times. Deal terms were not disclosed in the available material.

fbae9cff9d2d.why_it_matters: Local newspapers are a fragile corner of the media economy, and ownership changes can decide whether community coverage survives. A high-profile buyer with local roots could bring attention and stability, though the financial details are not yet known.

222e2ef667b3.headline: Blanche Plays Down Nvidia Questions as Chip Customers Face Scrutiny Over China Diversions
body: Blanche publicly downplayed questions about Nvidia, according to The New York Times, even as Justice Department investigators look into whether the company's high-powered computer chips have been illegally diverted to China by other firms.

The Times, citing people familiar with the inquiries, reports that investigators have gathered evidence of such diversions. The headline makes clear the scrutiny is falling on Nvidia's customers, not necessarily on the chipmaker itself. The material available does not detail who those customers are, how many chips are involved, or what charges might follow.

The contrast is the story: a reassuring public tone on one side, and an active evidence-gathering effort on the other. Those two things can coexist, since a company can be a supplier to firms under investigation without being accused of wrongdoing itself. But the gap is likely to draw attention in Washington.

Some context helps. The US has restricted exports of advanced AI chips to China, and enforcing those rules is notoriously hard. Chips are small, valuable and easy to move through intermediaries, which is why investigators tend to follow the resellers and middlemen rather than the manufacturer.

For Nvidia, whose processors sit at the heart of the AI boom, any enforcement push is worth watching. Cases against customers could bring tighter compliance demands on how chips are sold and tracked. We only have the Times' headline and teaser to go on, so many details remain unknown.

7c765ee92bba.headline: Sentences Served, Doors Still Shut: 48 Gaza Prisoners Held Past Their Release Dates
body: Forty-eight prisoners from Gaza remain in Israeli custody even though they have completed their sentences, according to the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs, as reported by Al Jazeera on November 25, 2026. Their families in Gaza are still waiting for them to come home.

Among them is Fadi Zughra, 43, a fisherman arrested at sea in August 2016 and accused of smuggling and sabotage, which his wife Shmou rejects. He finished an 8.5-year sentence in early 2025 but stayed locked up. Another is Hisham Harara, arrested in December 2015 at the Beit Hanoon (Erez) crossing while travelling to work in the West Bank. His nine-year sentence ended in December 2024, and his wife Hanan says the allegations relate to tunnels, despite his work in rubble removal and demolition.

Palestinian prisoners' organisations say Israel is using its Unlawful Combatants Law, passed in 2002, to keep holding people from Gaza. The law allows detention without a criminal conviction, subject to detention orders and judicial review. The practice raises questions about the legal basis for holding people after their terms have expired.

The cases sit within a broader rise in detentions. B'Tselem reported that the Israel Prison Service held 9,187 Palestinians on security grounds at the end of June 2026, including 1,554 from Gaza. Palestinian prisoners' institutions said in October that more than 9,400 were in custody, including 1,419 Gazans classified as unlawful combatants.

Rights groups and the UN have documented widespread abuse in detention, and the UN Human Rights Office said in September it had verified at least 92 deaths in Israeli custody since October 2023. The ICRC says it has been unable to visit detainees since the war began, which limits independent monitoring.

For the families the toll is personal. Hanan has raised seven children alone and keeps checking release lists despite her children's weariness. Shmou has four children, and says former prisoners relay word that Fadi is alive and asking after them. Both women say they simply want their husbands home.
7c765ee92bba.summary: Per Al Jazeera, 48 Gaza prisoners remain in Israeli custody after finishing their sentences, with groups pointing to the Unlawful Combatants Law. Families describe years of waiting and repeated false hopes.
7c765ee92bba.why_it_matters: Prolonged detention without conviction feeds legal and diplomatic pressure on Israel and complicates any lasting ceasefire or reconstruction arrangements in Gaza. Questions over due process can also affect international relations, aid politics and regional stability.
key_points: 48 Gaza prisoners remain held after completing sentences, per the Palestinian detainees commission.
Groups say Israel uses the 2002 Unlawful Combatants Law, which allows detention without conviction.
B'Tselem counted 1,554 Gazans among 9,187 Palestinians held on security grounds in June 2026.

Scale is the other eye-catcher. At 400 MW, this is a very large facility by any measure, in the territory of the big campuses built to serve cloud computing and artificial intelligence workloads. Demand for that kind of capacity has been a major driver of tech spending, and getting it online faster is a priority for operators.

5ce3ed5a9fcd.headline: Microsoft Calls a 'Code Red' After Its Worst-Ever Exchange Online Outage, and Yes, Teams Chats Were Involved
body: Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of how its engineers respond to incidents after the November 12 outage that cut users worldwide off from Exchange Online, Teams and Outlook, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters and reported by Ars Technica.

Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, reportedly described the event as the most customer-impacting in the history of Exchange Online. In another memo he wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. The target for the most urgent security fixes is one hour from detection to safe global deployment. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

Microsoft's post-incident report, dated November 20, blamed an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July that caused lock contention in gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then pushed extra load onto infrastructure that was already strained, since maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline.

Then came the "fog of war," a phrase used by Amanda Silver, a corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core. She wrote that responders swapped more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, scattering diagnostic data and fracturing the view of the incident. Charles Lamanna, an executive vice president, reportedly told a review that the affected component had piled up "roughly ten years' worth of acceptable failures."

Microsoft says the outage was not a cyberattack and the defects were not caused by AI tooling. The overhaul includes five workstreams covering load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery. Microsoft also plans to deploy its own AI agents to help engineers read system health data faster, and Henderson will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team.
The company has set one-hour goals for resolving major incidents and deploying urgent security fixes, but hasn't said when it expects to reach them.
5ce3ed5a9fcd.summary: Internal memos reported by Reuters show Microsoft launching a "Code Red" overhaul after the November 12 outage hit Exchange Online, Teams and Outlook, with one-hour recovery goals but no deadline.
5ce3ed5a9fcd.pixel_take: Eleven Teams chats and 11,000 messages to fix a Teams-related outage. Nothing says resilience like a group project where everyone is replying in a different thread.
5ce3ed5a9fcd.why_it_matters: Microsoft 365 underpins email and collaboration for countless businesses, so a long outage means lost productivity and tough questions about cloud concentration risk. How quickly Microsoft can patch and recover may influence customer trust and contract decisions.
key_points: Microsoft declared a "Code Red" after the November 12 outage, per Reuters-reviewed memos.
Cause: a Windows scalability defect from July, worsened by a Teams failover and about 14 percent of gateway capacity offline.
Targets of one-hour recovery and urgent-fix deployment have no stated timeline.

dd9641ab20f4.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Is Back as CEO, and Trump Says the AI Race Is Really a Talent War
body: Jensen Huang has returned as CEO of Nvidia, and the episode is being read as proof that the U.S.-China AI race is about people as much as chips, according to CNBC. Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He came back on Nov. 23, and Nvidia shares surged on the news.

President Donald Trump told CNBC he intervened to bring Huang back, saying the U.S. has to protect its geniuses. He warned that Huang could hypothetically have taken a job in China, though he acknowledged there was never even a suggestion that China had recruited him.

Analysts quoted by CNBC were split on how realistic that scenario is. Rui Ma of Tech Buzz China said Huang, as a founder, would more likely start his own company than manage someone else's. She also pointed to his deep belief in America and to laws that would stop him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese firm. Omdia's Lian Jye Su, however, said there is some truth to Trump's point given Huang's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain.

The broader talent picture is the real story. Carnegie Endowment research says China has overtaken the U.S. in share of global AI talent in just three years. Recruiter Rachel Wu said Chinese firms are aggressively hiring, citing a Meta engineer in Canada who took a Chinese startup offer of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000) plus stock options. Job hoppers can win pay bumps of 25% to 30%, and one ex-Alibaba engineer reportedly had more than five offers.

Money cuts both ways. U.S. engineers earn two or three times what Chinese peers do, so some companies mix markets and hire in China or Singapore. Meanwhile, U.S. chip export curbs of the past four years have not kept Chinese AI far behind, as DeepSeek showed in early 2025, though access to advanced chips still shapes where top researchers want to work.

Carnegie China's Damien Ma said he is watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving, though he expects limited policy change. Countries such as Singapore and South Korea could gain from a flow of AI talent.
dd9641ab20f4.summary: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO has sent shares higher and spotlighted a bigger contest: the U.S.-China fight for AI engineers, where China is gaining ground, according to CNBC.
dd9641ab20f4.pixel_take: Nvidia sold the world shovels for the AI gold rush, and it turns out the most valuable item in the shop was the guy with the leather jacket's brain, no export license required.
dd9641ab20f4.why_it_matters: Nvidia is a market heavyweight, and its shares jumped on a single leadership announcement, showing how much value rides on key people. If talent flows shift toward China or third countries, that could change where AI breakthroughs, and investment returns, come from.
key_points: Huang resigned Nov. 12 and returned Nov. 23, sending Nvidia shares surging.
Carnegie research says China now leads the U.S. in share of global AI talent.
U.S. engineers earn two to three times more than Chinese peers, pushing firms toward mixed hiring.

abf850cd2ca7.headline: China Shows Off 200kW Heavy-Fuel Aircraft Engine Built for Unmanned Aircraft
body: China has unveiled a 200-kilowatt heavy-fuel aircraft engine designed for unmanned aircraft, according to Interesting Engineering. The outlet reports that the engine is tied to a payload of about 2,200 pounds and a range of roughly 621 miles.

The teaser describes the engine as a more powerful domestic option for drones, with a range of possible applications. The full details were not available in the material we reviewed, so specifics such as the developer, the exact aircraft it will power and the timeline remain unclear.

The phrase heavy-fuel matters. Heavy-fuel engines run on fuels like diesel or kerosene-type fuel rather than gasoline. These fuels are generally less flammable and easier to handle and stock, which is why they are popular for logistics-minded aircraft that need to fly far and carry real cargo.

The numbers also suggest a leap in ambition. A payload of 2,200 pounds is well beyond what small consumer or camera drones can lift, and it puts such an aircraft in the category of larger cargo or utility platforms. A range of about 621 miles would let it cover long routes without a refuel stop.

The word domestic is the strategic part of the story. Building engines at home reduces reliance on imported powerplants, which have often been a bottleneck for countries scaling up their drone fleets. Whether this engine reaches mass production is something to watch, since a prototype on a stand and a reliable fleet in the sky are very different things.
abf850cd2ca7.summary: China has unveiled a 200kW heavy-fuel engine for unmanned aircraft, reportedly supporting a 2,200-pound payload and a 621-mile range, according to Interesting Engineering.

7a9297e644f4.headline: Istanbul's 'Loose Lioness' Turns Out Not to Be a Lioness, or Any Big Cat at All
body: Officials in Turkey now say an animal reported to be a lioness on the loose in Istanbul was not a lioness, a lion or any other kind of big cat, according to UPI.

The report had suggested a large predator was roaming free in the city, the kind of news that tends to clear sidewalks and fill group chats within minutes. The officials' updated assessment takes that scenario off the table.
The material available does not say what the animal actually was, who first spotted it, or how authorities reached their conclusion. We are not going to guess, though the internet certainly will.

The episode is a reminder of how quickly an unverified sighting can spread, and how a dramatic label can stick before anyone has checked it. Big-cat alerts are the sort of claim that travels faster than the facts, and corrections usually arrive a step behind.
For now, the takeaway from the Turkish officials is simple: whatever was seen in Istanbul, it was not a lion, and residents can set aside that particular fear.
7a9297e644f4.summary: Turkish officials now believe an animal reported as a lioness on the loose in Istanbul was not a lion, lioness or any other big cat, UPI reported.
7a9297e644f4.pixel_take: Officials have confirmed the beast was not a lioness, which is great news for Istanbul and mildly disappointing for everyone who already drafted the dramatic group-chat message.
7a9297e644f4.why_it_matters: The story is a small example of how fast unverified claims spread and how slowly corrections follow, a dynamic that also moves markets and shapes consumer decisions. Checking the source before reacting is a habit that pays off, whether the topic is a wild animal or a hot stock tip.

They also ruled out any other variety of big cat, according to UPI.
What the animal actually was has not been stated in the available material.

a87455069b89.headline: Kilmar Ábrego García Leaves US for Spain, Ending Long Deportation Fight Over Trump's Immigration Agenda
body: Kilmar Ábrego García, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador in 2025 turned into one of the most closely watched immigration fights in the US, has left the country for Spain, according to BBC News. The report was published on 25 November 2026.

Ábrego García, who lived in Maryland and is married to a US citizen, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager. After his 2019 arrest, a judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there. In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him anyway, and he was held in the Cecot prison, known for harsh conditions.

The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return. The administration admitted the deportation was an error and brought him back to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying he had been charged for political reasons.

The saga did not end there. The administration kept trying to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana. Ábrego García had said he would accept deportation to Costa Rica, which had agreed to take him as a refugee with legal status. After reports of a possible Uganda transfer, a judge barred deportation to any third country. CBS reported that the administration at one point asked the judge to lift that order so it could send him to Liberia.

Maryland Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, who visited him in Cecot in 2025, said Ábrego García is now travelling to a country of his choice as a free man. His lawyer called the departure temporary, said they do not expect a return under this administration, and hope the next one will reunite him with his family in Maryland. The BBC has asked the Department of Homeland Security for comment.
a87455069b89.summary: Kilmar Ábrego García, wrongly deported to El Salvador in 2025 and later returned to the US, has left for Spain. His lawyer calls the move temporary and hopes the next administration will allow his return.
a87455069b89.why_it_matters: The case shows how courts can constrain executive immigration powers, and how costly and drawn-out such legal battles can become for governments and individuals. It remains a political marker for debates over immigration enforcement heading into future elections.
key_points: Ábrego García left the US for Spain, a country of his choosing, per BBC News.
His 2025 deportation to El Salvador was admitted to be an error; human trafficking charges against him were later dismissed.
His lawyer calls the departure temporary and hopes the next administration will allow his return to Maryland.

df3bc2124137.headline: Tokyo Stocks Take a Tumble as Nikkei 225 Sheds 2.62% by the Close
body: Japanese equities finished lower on the day, with the benchmark Nikkei 225 index down 2.62% at the close of trade in Tokyo, according to Investing.com.
That is a sizeable one-day move for a major index. Drops of more than 2% tend to get traders' attention, even if they don't automatically signal a deeper trend.

The material available gives only the headline figure. It does not say what drove the decline, which sectors or companies led it, or how the yen, bond yields or other Asian markets behaved. Without that detail, it would be guesswork to pin the fall on any single cause.

For context, the Nikkei 225 is a price-weighted index of 225 large Japanese companies and is widely watched as a barometer of the country's stock market. Because it is price-weighted, big moves in a handful of high-priced shares can swing it noticeably.

Investors will likely watch whether the weakness carries into the next session or fades, and whether other regional markets show similar moves. For now, the one firm fact is the number: down 2.62% at the bell.

f3c91c81ff9b.headline: Genspark's VoicePad gives your AI a five-button remote, with mechanical switches for the keyboard-snob in all of us
body: Genspark, the Palo Alto company behind Genspark AI Workspace, has unveiled the SecondBrain VoicePad, a palm-sized aluminum gadget with five keys and two microphones, according to Yanko Design. Press a key, speak, and your words appear wherever your cursor is blinking on a Mac or PC.

The pitch rests on simple math: the average person types around 40 words a minute but speaks closer to 160. That gap is the basis for Genspark's "up to 4x faster" claim, which is about input speed, not a promise of finished writing. The pad weighs 85 grams, has a CNC-machined body, and connects over Bluetooth or USB-C.

Out of the box the keys cover dictation, meeting notes, calendar, slides and Genspark's AI agent. All can be remapped to launch apps such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Notion or Slack, or to run shortcuts like Copy, Paste and Enter. Beneath them sit Cherry MX Ultra Low Profile tactile switches, rated for more than 50 million keystrokes.

Genspark says voice typing works in more than 100 apps and cleans up filler words, and that whispered dictation works when the device is held close to your mouth. A translate key supports speech in more than 50 languages, but output is English only. The device can also record meetings on its own, with no laptop needed, and Genspark says it records only when a key is pressed and has no wake word. Battery life is rated at about 20 hours.

The price comes with strings. A year of unlimited voice typing and translation, 1,000 Super Agent credits and 300 minutes of monthly meeting transcription are included. After year one, dictation falls to a free allowance of 4,000 words a week, and translation costs 1 credit per minute. Planned retail is $169, with early Kickstarter pricing from $99, and warranty terms have not been published.
f3c91c81ff9b.summary: Genspark's SecondBrain VoicePad is a five-key aluminum gadget with Cherry mechanical switches that turns speech into text and triggers AI apps. Retail is planned at $169, with Kickstarter pricing from $99.
f3c91c81ff9b.pixel_take: A $169 gadget so you can talk to your computer instead of typing. The keyboard isn't fired, just given a very chatty coworker who also wants to run your meetings.
f3c91c81ff9b.why_it_matters: Voice is becoming a main way to drive AI tools, and companies are pairing software subscriptions with dedicated hardware. The one-year bundle then credit-based pricing shows how the real cost of AI gadgets may sit in the ongoing service, not the device.
key_points: VoicePad has five remappable Cherry MX ULP keys, two microphones and an 85-gram aluminum body.
It dictates, translates into English and records meetings offline, with about 20 hours of battery.
Planned price is $169, with Kickstarter from $99; free perks shrink after year one.

886e6fb7c86d.headline: Trump reportedly open to pardoning Nvidia's Jensen Huang before Senate testimony, as Schumer alleges export violations
body: A live blog from The Guardian, published on 25 November 2026, reports that Donald Trump has said he is open to pardoning Jensen Huang ahead of the CEO's planned testimony before a Senate committee. The wording is "reportedly", so the claim rests on the Guardian's account rather than a formal announcement.

According to the Guardian, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer accused Huang of violating US export control laws. The accusation relates to shipments of chips to China. The teaser does not say what evidence Schumer cited, and it does not indicate that any charges have been filed.

The teaser also notes that Trump was taking part in a Medal of Freedom ceremony earlier in the day. The material available does not say how the pardon remark was made or in what context, so those details remain unclear.

A little context helps here. Export controls limit which advanced semiconductors US companies can sell to China, and they have become a central tool in the technology rivalry between the two countries. Chips sit at the heart of artificial intelligence, which is why the rules draw so much scrutiny in Congress.

A presidential pardon would normally follow a conviction or at least a federal charge, so floating one before any such step is unusual. Still, the material we have is thin, and the full details of the exchange are not available. We will update if more emerges.
886e6fb7c86d.summary: The Guardian reports Trump said he is open to pardoning Nvidia's Jensen Huang before his Senate testimony, while Chuck Schumer accused Huang of violating export control laws over chip shipments to China.
886e6fb7c86d.pixel_take: Offering a pardon before the testimony even starts is like handing out an umbrella before anyone checks the forecast. Senators will surely have questions about the weather.
886e6fb7c86d.why_it_matters: Chip export rules shape how much advanced AI hardware reaches China, and any legal or political fight over them can move technology stocks and supply chains. Investors in chipmakers watch these disputes closely because they affect revenue and regulatory risk.
key_points: The Guardian reports Trump is open to pardoning Jensen Huang.
Chuck Schumer accused Huang of violating US export control laws over chip shipments to China.
Huang is due to testify before a Senate committee.

738443e67a1f.headline: US readies new tariff round on 14 trading partners, after the last one got tossed out in court
body: The United States is preparing to announce new tariffs on a group of trading partners as early as Wednesday, according to BBC News, which says it understands the plan is in the works. At least 14 jurisdictions would be affected, including China, the European Union and Japan.

The move follows the White House's "Section 301" investigation, launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal. In other words, the administration is trying a different door after the first one was slammed shut by the courts.

Under the plan, countries would face different import tax rates depending on the deals they have previously struck with Trump. The BBC notes that Trump has made tariffs a signature policy, arguing they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has argued that overproduction abroad displaces American factories and deters investment.

The timing is delicate for relations with China. Despite a meeting last week between Trump and President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, the two sides have not fully settled their differences, and an interim agreement is set to expire on 10 January. Washington had accused Beijing of falling short on commitments from October 2025, particularly on agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals.

There was one conciliatory signal from Beijing. Earlier on Tuesday, China extended its suspension of a ban on exports of critical minerals including gallium, germanium and antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have started on Friday.

Critics say the administration's tariff policy has pushed up prices for American consumers and hurt the global economy. The BBC also links to a report that the administration has paid back $100bn in Liberation Day tariffs to businesses.
738443e67a1f.summary: The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on at least 14 jurisdictions, including China, the EU and Japan, as early as Wednesday, BBC News reports, after the Supreme Court struck down the earlier Liberation Day tariffs.
738443e67a1f.pixel_take: When the court says no to one tariff plan, the answer is apparently a new tariff plan with a different legal name tag. Trade policy as a game of whack-a-mole.
738443e67a1f.why_it_matters: Import taxes tend to filter into consumer prices and company costs, so a new tariff round matters for household budgets and corporate earnings. Uncertainty over rates also makes it harder for businesses to plan supply chains, and it can rattle markets, especially with the US-China truce due to expire in January.
key_points: New tariffs could be announced as early as Wednesday, hitting at least 14 jurisdictions including China, the EU and Japan.
The plan follows a Section 301 probe launched after the Supreme Court struck down the Liberation Day tariffs.
US-China tensions remain high, with an interim deal expiring on 10 January.

b9a6c473148d.headline: UK Energy Bills Jump 26% in January as Iran War Lifts Gas Prices
body: Energy bills for millions of UK households will rise by 26% from January, regulator Ofgem announced, blaming a surge in wholesale gas prices driven largely by the Iran war, according to BBC News.

For a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales paying by direct debit, the annual bill would go from £1,723 to £2,166 if the new price cap level lasted a full year. That works out at about £37 more a month in the first three months of 2027. Ofgem said actual costs will depend on how much energy each home uses during the coldest part of the year.

Ofgem said the cap, which is reset every three months, rose entirely because suppliers face higher wholesale costs. It is the biggest increase since Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed prices up. Households on prepayment meters may feel it most, as their spending peaks when they need the most energy.

The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January, on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity. Equivalent payments will apply in Scotland and Wales. Separately, the warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits. Citizens Advice chief executive Dame Clare Moriarty warned of "a brutal winter", and the charity said the money will vanish quickly, especially for prepayment customers. Energy UK said the support was poorly targeted and too small to stop customer debt rising.

Politics is already heating up. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said families have paid the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets. Shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie blamed Labour for piling green levies and taxes onto bills. Ofgem has told suppliers to spot struggling customers early, make help easy to reach and keep repayment plans affordable.
b9a6c473148d.summary: Ofgem says the price cap will rise 26% in January, taking a typical annual bill from £1,723 to £2,166, as the Iran war lifts wholesale gas costs. Government support is coming, but charities say it won't be enough.
b9a6c473148d.why_it_matters: Higher energy bills squeeze household budgets just as winter demand peaks, which can dent spending elsewhere and push up debt. It also keeps pressure on inflation and puts the UK's exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets back in focus.
key_points: Ofgem's cap rises 26% in January, taking a typical annual bill from £1,723 to £2,166.
The increase is the largest since the price spike after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
A £100 payment and £150 warm home discount offer help, but charities warn it will not go far.

aee304b6b072.headline: Czech central bank bought bitcoin a year ago, and it's keeping quiet about what the stash is worth
body: The Czech National Bank (CNB) bought bitcoin about a year ago as an experiment, and it is now declining to say what the holding is worth, according to CoinDesk. The report comes as the price of bitcoin has fallen by at least 40% since the purchase.

The bank's audited accounts carry the coins at cost rather than at market value. That is a legitimate way to present an asset, but it means the official books do not show the paper loss that the market price implies. Anyone looking at the accounts alone would not see the damage.

The CNB also told CoinDesk that an outside custodian holds the coins. In other words, the central bank is not guarding private keys itself but relies on a third-party provider to keep the assets safe.

The teaser does not say how large the purchase was, and the bank has not put a current figure on it. That leaves a gap: we know the direction of the price move, but not the size of the exposure in money terms.

The episode is a useful test case for how a conservative institution handles a volatile asset. Central banks typically hold reserves that are meant to be stable and liquid, and bitcoin's swings sit awkwardly with that mandate. Labeling the purchase an experiment gives the CNB room to frame any loss as tuition rather than a bet gone wrong, though transparency about the results is what would make the experiment informative.
aee304b6b072.summary: The Czech National Bank bought bitcoin a year ago as an experiment. The coin is down at least 40% since, the audited accounts show it at cost, and the bank won't say what it's worth, CoinDesk reports.
aee304b6b072.pixel_take: A central bank ran a bitcoin experiment, and now the results are classified. Science usually likes to publish the data, especially when the data goes down 40%.
aee304b6b072.why_it_matters: Central bank interest in bitcoin is a signal for how mainstream crypto has become, but opaque reporting undercuts the case for it as a reserve asset. Cost-based accounting can hide losses, so taxpayers and markets get an incomplete picture of what public institutions are risking.
key_points: The Czech National Bank bought bitcoin about a year ago as an experiment.
Bitcoin has fallen at least 40% since, yet the audited accounts carry it at cost.
The CNB says an outside custodian holds the coins and has not disclosed their current value.

358e19644976.headline: One in Four University of Bath Survey Respondents Used AI for Mental Health Support
body: A survey by the University of Bath, published in JMIR Mental Health, found that 25% of students who responded had used generative AI for mental health support in the past six months, according to Digital Trends. The team contacted all 22,207 enrolled students and heard back from 2,020, a response rate of about 9.1%.

Of those respondents, 503 said yes. Some 19.3% said they sought quick advice during emotionally hard moments, while others used AI to understand their mental health or as a stand-in therapist or coach. Fifty-four students, or 2.7%, said they used it while having thoughts of self-harm.

The paper stresses that generative AI tools are not designed, regulated or clinically validated to deliver mental health treatment or crisis intervention. Digital Trends also notes that OpenAI has reported a small share of weekly ChatGPT users show signs of suicidal planning or intent.

Use was higher among those struggling. About 36.8% of students reporting very low well-being used the tools, versus 19.1% of those with average well-being. Usage was also higher among students with declared disabilities and those aged 26 to 29. The researchers suggest AI is acting as an informal support system, helped by the fact that a chatbot answers instantly, even in the middle of the night.

There are caveats. The low response rate may inflate the headline figure if struggling students were likelier to reply, women were overrepresented, and the work covered a single UK campus. The study cannot say whether poor well-being drives AI use, or the reverse, or whether both reflect unmet needs for support.

The researchers are expanding into a national, multi-university study. The University of Bath has issued guidelines for students using these tools, and OpenAI now lets adults name someone to be contacted if a chat raises serious self-harm concerns.
358e19644976.summary: A University of Bath survey found 25% of responding students used generative AI for mental health support in six months, including some during thoughts of self-harm. Researchers caution about the low response rate and single campus.
358e19644976.why_it_matters: As chatbots become default confidants, tech companies face pressure over safety features and regulation for tools never built for clinical care. Universities and employers may need to rethink support services, since demand for accessible help is clearly going unmet.
key_points: 503 of 2,020 respondents (25.0%) used generative AI for mental health support in six months.
Use reached 36.8% among students with very low well-being versus 19.1% with average well-being.
Low 9.1% response rate and a single campus mean the figure may be overstated; a national study is planned.

4efcf4fe63e1.headline: Australia Passes Law Forcing Internet Platforms to Pull Harmful Content
body: Australia has passed a law requiring internet platforms to take down harmful content, according to a headline from Investing.com published on November 25, 2026.

The material available is limited to that headline, so details such as which platforms are covered, how harmful content is defined, the deadlines for removal and the penalties for non-compliance are not known at this stage.

Even so, the direction of travel is clear. Governments around the world have been moving from asking tech companies to police themselves toward writing binding rules that say what must come down. Australia has been among the more active countries in this area, and a new law adds to the pressure on large platforms to build and fund moderation systems.

For the companies involved, such rules typically mean higher compliance costs, more staff and automated tools for review, and legal exposure if they get it wrong. Critics of laws like this usually raise concerns about free expression and about how broadly harm gets defined, while supporters argue that voluntary efforts have not been enough.
We will update this story if more details on the scope and enforcement of the law become available.
4efcf4fe63e1.summary: Australia has passed a law requiring internet platforms to remove harmful content, per Investing.com. Details on scope, deadlines and penalties were not available in the material.
4efcf4fe63e1.pixel_take: Australia has told the internet to tidy its room. Now comes the hard part: agreeing on what counts as mess.
4efcf4fe63e1.why_it_matters: Binding takedown rules can raise compliance costs for large platforms and add legal risk, which investors in tech companies watch closely. They also signal a wider regulatory trend that could shape how online services operate across markets.
key_points: Australia has passed a law requiring platforms to remove harmful content.
Details on scope, deadlines and penalties were not provided in the material.
The move fits a global trend toward binding rules for tech companies.

9d6bab0e9cb5.headline: UK Tells Ukraine-Linked Firms: Lock Up, Russian Saboteurs May Come Calling
body: Britain's Ministry of Defence and the National Protective Security Authority, which is part of the MI5 security service, issued an unusual public warning on Tuesday. Companies that support Ukraine's military could face attempted sabotage from Russia, according to Al Jazeera.

The notice said any organisation involved in military procurement or supplying equipment to Ukraine's armed forces could be a target. It described the activity as typically involving proxy actors using low-sophistication methods such as arson, and urged firms to act against the threat from operatives working for Russia.

Russia's embassy in London rejected the claims, saying Russia has no plans, reasons or intentions to attack the UK. It accused Ukraine of staging sabotage to blame Moscow and extract more money from Western governments, a charge Kyiv has repeatedly denied.

The warning follows a string of incidents. Last year three British men were convicted over an arson attack on a warehouse storing Starlink satellite equipment bound for Ukraine, which prosecutors said was carried out for Russian military intelligence. In September, a man was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service after alleged contact with Russian military spies.

The wider region is on edge too. Estonia said on Sunday it would close all its border crossings with Russia after a suspected sabotage attack on an Estonian defence company. Last week Norway's security service said it expected Russian intelligence to attempt sabotage there in the coming year.

The Ministry of Defence said it is holding closed-door briefings over two days with leaders from critical national infrastructure and defence sectors. Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent attempts across Europe show how serious the threats are, and called the targeting of organisations aiding Ukraine shameful.
9d6bab0e9cb5.summary: UK defence and security officials publicly warned firms supporting Ukraine's military that Russia-linked proxies may try sabotage such as arson. Moscow denies it, as Europe reports more suspected incidents.
9d6bab0e9cb5.why_it_matters: Defence suppliers and infrastructure operators may need to spend more on physical security, which can raise costs and insurance premiums. Sabotage risk also adds to geopolitical uncertainty for European markets and supply chains tied to the Ukraine war.
key_points: UK defence officials and MI5's protective security arm warned firms supplying Ukraine they could be sabotage targets.
Russia denied the claims and blamed Ukraine, which Kyiv rejects.
Estonia and Norway have also flagged suspected or expected Russian sabotage.

81b3bc3d194e.headline: China Reportedly Eyes Airline Mergers and Tougher Rules to Lift Its Struggling Carriers
body: China is considering airline mergers and tougher industry rules as a way to help struggling carriers, according to a report from the South China Morning Post, as relayed by Investing.com on November 25, 2026.

The material available is limited to that headline, so details are thin. It does not say which airlines might be combined, what the stricter rules would cover, who is driving the plan, or when anything could happen. Those gaps matter, and we are not going to fill them with guesses.

Even so, the direction of travel is easy to follow. Mergers are a classic remedy when too many players chase the same passengers and margins get squeezed. Fewer, larger carriers can trim overlapping routes, share costs and gain pricing discipline. Tougher rules, meanwhile, usually aim to curb behavior such as aggressive fare cutting, though the report as summarized does not say that is the intent here.

For investors, consolidation talk tends to move sentiment around listed airlines, since the winners and losers of any deal shape valuations. Travelers could see changes too, from fares to route choices, though that is general industry logic rather than anything stated in the report.

For now, treat this as a signal rather than a plan. Nothing in the available material confirms a formal announcement, so the next step to watch is whether officials or the airlines themselves comment.
81b3bc3d194e.summary: The South China Morning Post reports that China is weighing airline mergers and stricter rules to help struggling carriers. Details such as names, timing and scope were not available.
