Animal rescuers are preparing a weight loss plan for the dog.
Further details on the dog's health were not provided.

2b702663be1a.headline: WhatsApp Stickers Are Getting a Voice, but They'll Stay Muted Until You Tap
body: WhatsApp is reportedly rolling out sound stickers to select Android beta testers, according to Digital Trends, citing a report from WABetaInfo. The feature turns short video clips into animated stickers that carry audio, and it arrives after months of internal testing.

Making one starts in the sticker keyboard. You tap the option to create a sticker, pick a video from your gallery, and WhatsApp converts it into an animated sticker. A new audio button appears at the top of the editor, opening a screen with four ways to add a soundtrack: keep the video's original audio, choose a built-in sound effect, record a voice clip, or import a saved track from the Files app.

The voice recorder reportedly runs up to five seconds. Each sound sticker carries a small audio icon, and playback is muted by default, so a group chat won't suddenly erupt. Recipients hear the sound only if they tap the icon, after which the track loops three times and stops. According to the report, end-to-end encryption covers both the animation and its sound.

Android users in the beta program can look for WhatsApp version 2.26.47.1 via the Google Play Store, though the audio button will appear gradually over the coming weeks, so installing the build doesn't guarantee access. An iOS beta, version 26.46.10.70, also includes sound stickers with preset effects such as Cat Purr, Crickets and Weird Kid Laugh.
There is no word on when the feature will reach everyone. For now it sits somewhere between a reaction meme and a full voice message, with the volume knob firmly in the listener's hands.
2b702663be1a.summary: WhatsApp is reportedly testing sound stickers with Android beta users, letting people add audio to video-based stickers. Sound stays muted until a recipient taps, and the content is end-to-end encrypted.
2b702663be1a.pixel_take: Finally, a way to send a cricket chirp to a dead group chat. The mute-by-default design is the real hero: your coworkers' 'Weird Kid Laugh' stays off until you consent.
2b702663be1a.why_it_matters: Messaging apps compete on small expressive features that keep people inside their ecosystems, and WhatsApp's moves here show how it keeps its huge user base engaged. Tap-to-play audio also shows how privacy and etiquette shape product design when features meet crowded group chats.
key_points: Sound stickers are reaching select Android beta testers, per WABetaInfo via Digital Trends.
Audio can come from the video, built-in effects, a 5-second recording or a saved file.
Playback is muted until tapped, loops three times, and is end-to-end encrypted.

53f5c40312e6.headline: Huawei Found Guilty by U.S. Federal Jury in Sanctions and Trade Secrets Case
body: A federal jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies and its subsidiaries guilty of violating U.S. sanctions on Iran and stealing American trade secrets, according to The Hill. The report, published on November 25, 2026, describes the verdict as a major development in a long-running American legal fight against the company.

The material available to us is brief, and it doesn't spell out sentencing, fines, the full list of counts, or how Huawei plans to respond. Those details will matter a great deal, so readers should expect more to emerge as the case moves past the verdict.

What the verdict does signal is that a U.S. jury accepted prosecutors' claims on two separate fronts: that the company broke American sanctions rules tied to Iran, and that it took trade secrets belonging to American firms. Sanctions violations and intellectual property theft are exactly the sort of accusations Washington has leveled at Chinese tech companies for years.

The case sits inside the wider technology rivalry between the United States and China, where telecom equipment, chips and data security have become geopolitical bargaining chips. A guilty verdict gives U.S. officials a court-tested argument when they press allies and businesses to limit dealings with Huawei.

For companies, the practical lesson is old but sharp: sanctions compliance is not optional, and a global supply chain can turn into a legal minefield. Expect lawyers, compliance teams and trade-policy watchers to read every line of whatever comes next.
53f5c40312e6.summary: A U.S. federal jury found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating Iran sanctions and stealing American trade secrets, The Hill reports. Sentencing and Huawei's response were not detailed.
53f5c40312e6.pixel_take: Huawei has now learned the hard way that a jury, unlike a supply chain, can't be rerouted through a friendly third country.
53f5c40312e6.why_it_matters: A guilty verdict strengthens Washington's hand in its tech standoff with China and may push companies and allies to rethink ties with Huawei. It also reminds businesses that sanctions and IP violations carry real legal and financial risk, which can affect supply chains and investor confidence.
key_points: A U.S. federal jury found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty, per The Hill.
The charges include violating Iran sanctions and stealing American trade secrets.
Sentencing details and Huawei's response were not in the available report.
